Title: Supernodes and Halos: Loss-Critical Hubs in LLM Feed-Forward Layers
Text:
Supernodes and Halos: Loss-Critical Hubs in LLM Feed-Forward Layers
Audrey Cherilyn, Houman Safaai1
Kempner Institute at Harvard University
Abstract
We study the organization of channel-level im-
portance in transformer feed-forward networks
(FFNs). Using a Fisher-style loss proxy (LP)
based on activation-gradient second moments, we
show that loss sensitivity is concentrated in a
small set of channels within each layer. In Llama-
3.1-8B, the top 1% of channels per layer accounts
for a median of 58.7% of LP mass (range: 33.0–
86.1%). We call these loss-critical channels su-
pernodes.
Although FFN layers also contain
strong activation outliers, LP-defined supernodes
overlap only weakly with activation-defined out-
liers and are not explained by activation power
or weight norms alone. Around this core, we
find a weaker but consistent halo structure: some
non-supernode channels share the supernodes’
write support and show stronger redundancy with
the protected core. We use one-shot structured
FFN pruning as a diagnostic test of this organiza-
tion. At 50% FFN sparsity, baselines that prune
many supernodes degrade sharply, whereas our
SCAR variants explicitly protect the supernode
core; the strongest variant, SCAR-Prot, reaches
perplexity 54.8 compared with 989.2 for Wanda-
channel. The LP-concentration pattern appears
across Mistral-7B, Llama-2-7B, and Qwen2-7B,
remains visible in targeted Llama-3.1-70B exper-
iments, and increases during OLMo-2-7B pre-
training. These results suggest that LLM FFNs
develop a small learned core of loss-critical chan-
nels, and that preserving this core is important for
reliable structured pruning.

to carry disproportionate functional importance. Prior work

channels. That is exactly where quality often drops.
We study the intermediate channels of FFN layers, which
account for a large share of parameters in modern decoder
LLMs and are a natural target for structured compression
(Touvron et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Jiang et al.,
2023; Yang et al., 2024). Our starting observation is that
loss sensitivity across FFN channels is extremely uneven.
Using a Fisher-style proxy that combines activations with
gradient information, we find that the top 1% of channels
per layer captures between 33.0% and 86.1% of the total
sensitivity mass (median 58.7%). We call these channels
supernodes. Their sensitivity can exceed the layer mean by
roughly three orders of magnitude, and often by more.
Supernodes are not merely statistical outliers: targeted abla-
tions indicate that they are functionally critical. When we
force a pruning mask to remove them, perplexity jumps from
6.2 to over 8 × 105, even at only 50% sparsity (Appendix
Table A5). Removing the same number of non-supernode
channels is far less damaging. This points to one common
failure mode of aggressive structured pruning: many meth-
ods eventually hit a very small set of channels that the model
relies on heavily.
Because LP is estimated on calibration data, we also sep-
arate two notions of stability. The phenomenon is stable:
extreme LP concentration appears across calibration do-
mains. The identities are less stable: the specific top-LP
channels are domain-conditioned. In practice, this means
that SCAR should be calibrated on data representative of the
intended deployment domain.
After identifying the supernode core, we ask whether
nearby non-core channels contain structure that can guide
pruning. Within each layer, channels with overlapping
high-magnitude coordinates in their Wdown columns clus-
ter around supernodes, forming what we call write halos.
These halo channels show measurable redundancy with re-
spect to the protected supernode core. Across layers, chan-
nels in the next layer that read heavily from the supernode
output support form read halos. We use halo structure as
a secondary refinement, not as the main explanation for
pruning behavior.
We then use structured pruning as a functional test of this
structure. At 50% FFN channel sparsity on Llama-3.1-8B,
the baselines in Table 1 remove roughly 20–42% of su-
pernodes and degrade to perplexities of several hundred to
several thousand. Methods that protect all supernodes retain
substantially lower perplexity: our best variant, SCAR-Prot,
reaches perplexity 54.8, compared with 989.2 for channel-
adapted Wanda. Across methods, supernode hit-rate is
strongly associated with perplexity, and controlled random-
mask sweeps show a clear dose-response trend.
1.1. Contributions
Our contributions are fourfold. Together, they show that
FFN importance is concentrated in a small loss-critical core
and that preserving this core is often the difference between
stable and unstable structured pruning. First, we define a
Fisher-style channel loss proxy for FFN channels and use it
to identify supernodes: the top 1% of channels by loss sen-
sitivity. We show that these channels account for a large frac-
tion of LP mass and that ablating them is far more damag-
ing than ablating comparable non-supernode sets. Second,
we show that supernode hit-rate explains a major failure
mode of one-shot structured FFN pruning. Methods that re-
move more supernodes degrade more sharply, and controlled
random-mask sweeps show a dose–response relationship
between supernode removal and perplexity. Third, we char-
acterize secondary halo structure around the supernode core.
Write-halo channels share supernode write support and show
higher redundancy with the protected core, while read-halo
diagnostics suggest modest cross-layer dependence on the
same support. Fourth, we validate LP concentration and
core protection across Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Llama-2-
7B, Qwen2-7B, targeted Llama-3.1-70B experiments, and
OLMo-2-7B training checkpoints, where LP concentration
increases during pretraining.
2. Background and Related Work
We first fix the channel-level notation used throughout the
paper, then relate our work to three nearby lines of research:
activation outliers, critical individual weights, and structured
pruning. Supernodes sit between these prior phenomena.
They are not individual weights, but they are also not generic
activation outliers; they are structured FFN channels whose
importance is defined through loss sensitivity.

2.2. Outlier Phenomena in LLMs
Several recent results suggest that rare components can have
disproportionate influence in LLM computation. These com-
ponents have been studied at different granularities, from
activation coordinates to individual weights. We review
them because they motivate the central question of this pa-
per: whether an analogous concentration exists at the level
of whole FFN channels.
Massive activations.
Sun et al. (2024a) show that a small
number of activation coordinates exhibit unusually large
values that behave like implicit bias terms and can create at-
tention sinks. We study FFN intermediate channels instead,
defining supernodes by loss sensitivity rather than activation
magnitude.
Outliers in quantization.
Activation outliers are also cen-
tral to LLM quantization: LLM.int8() isolates outlier feature
dimensions in higher precision (Dettmers et al., 2022), and
SmoothQuant reduces activation outlier difficulty by shift-
ing scale from activations to weights (Xiao et al., 2023).
These works show that outlier structure matters for com-
pression. They do not, however, identify a channel-level
loss-critical FFN core or test its role in structured pruning.
Super weights.
Yu et al. (2024) identify individual weight
parameters whose removal destroys model output. They
show that as few as a single super weight can be critical, and
that super weights induce corresponding super activations.
In contrast, we focus on structured FFN channels spanning
rows and columns across projections, identify them by loss
sensitivity, and characterize their halo neighborhoods.
Prior work shows that outlier activations and individual
critical weights can strongly affect LLM behavior and com-
pression. We extend this line of evidence to structured FFN
channels. Specifically, we show that second-order channel
sensitivity is concentrated in a small loss-critical core, that
ablating this core is highly damaging, and that protecting
it substantially improves one-shot structured FFN pruning.
Halo structure provides an additional local signal for rank-
ing non-core channels, but the primary contribution is the
identification and validation of the supernode core.
2.3. Structured Pruning of LLMs
Pruning provides both a practical compression tool and a
diagnostic for understanding which parts of a model are
functionally important. In this paper, we use pruning in the
second sense as well as the first: if a small set of channels is
truly loss-critical, then pruning methods that remove those
channels should fail more sharply than methods that protect
them. Structured FFN pruning therefore gives a natural
testbed for studying supernodes.
Unstructured pruning.
Wanda (Sun et al., 2024b) scores
weights by |w|·|x| and achieves strong unstructured sparsity.
SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023) uses second-order
information for one-shot weight removal. These methods
excel at fine-grained sparsity but do not yield hardware
speedups without specialized sparse kernels.

Structured pruning.
Group Fisher Pruning (Liu et al.,
2021) uses Fisher information to score parameter groups
for removal in CNNs, establishing that group-level Fisher
sensitivity is an effective structured pruning criterion. LLM-
Pruner (Ma et al., 2023) performs structural pruning with
LoRA recovery. OWL (Yin et al., 2024) extends Wanda
with outlier-aware non-uniform layer-wise sparsity alloca-
tion. OATS (Zhang & Papyan, 2025) decomposes weights
into sparse + low-rank terms. The novelty here is not Fisher-
based scoring itself, but the observation that such scoring
reveals extreme concentration in a small channel subset (su-
pernodes), and that protecting this subset accounts for much
of the sharp pruning gap we observe. However, aggressive
FFN channel removal (our focus) remains challenging in
one-shot settings: at 50% channel sparsity, standard channel-
adapted methods can suffer severe perplexity degradation.
Why channel pruning is hard.
We argue that part of the
difficulty comes from supernode structure. The loss-critical
core is so small that pruning rules not designed to protect it
can remove many supernodes while still looking reasonable
under aggregate saliency. Once a method removes even
a modest fraction of this core, model quality can degrade
sharply.

Why does concentration emerge?
LP concentration is
not explained by activation magnitude or curvature alone. In
Appendix Fig. A9, we decompose LP into activation-only,
curvature-only, factorized activation–curvature, and exact
activation–gradient terms. Exact LP is more concentrated
than the simpler baselines, especially at 70B scale, sug-
gesting that supernodes arise from joint activation–gradient
structure rather than from activation outliers alone. Because
the per-layer summaries and the 8B/70B factor comparison
use different aggregation protocols, percentages should only
be compared within the same protocol.
Calibration-domain stability.
We distinguish two no-
tions of stability: phenomenon stability (does extreme LP
concentration occur?) and identity stability (are the same
channels identified?). Across the four calibration domains
we test (WikiText-2, C4, code, and arXiv), extreme LP
concentration appears consistently, with per-layer top-1%
mass in the same broad range as the main WikiText-2 anal-
ysis. However, the specific channel identities are domain-
conditioned: mean pairwise Jaccard overlap is only ≈6%
at the 1% supernode fraction. This instability is not the
same as activation-defined outliers: even within a single
domain, the top-1% LP and activation-defined channel
sets overlap only weakly (Fig. 2D), although activation-
defined supernodes can still serve as an effective protected-
set surrogate when SCAR’s pruning score is held fixed (Ap-
pendix §D.4). Activation-defined supernodes are more sta-
ble across domains, whereas LP-defined supernodes better
reflect domain-specific loss sensitivity (Appendix §D.4).
This reinforces the practical recommendation that SCAR
should be calibrated on data representative of the intended
deployment domain.
4. Write-Halo Structure
Having identified the loss-critical core, we next ask whether
the remaining channels are locally structured around it. This
analysis has a narrower role than the supernode result: it
looks for signals that may help rank non-supernode channels
once the core is protected. We call these neighborhoods
halos, defined by write-pattern overlap (Eq. 6) together with
redundancy diagnostics.
We distinguish two related concepts. A write halo consists
of channels within the same layer whose write vectors over-
lap with the supernode-defined write support. This is the
halo object used in the pruning diagnostics. A read coupling
effect occurs when channels in the next layer concentrate
their read weights on the supernode output support, provid-
ing a mechanistic link across layers.

6. Validation: Structured Pruning as a Probe
If supernodes capture genuine functional organization, prun-
ing strategies that preserve them should be more robust than
otherwise similar strategies that remove them. We use struc-
tured FFN channel pruning to test this claim quantitatively,
with halo features treated as a secondary refinement after
the core is protected.
6.1. Pruning Framework: SCAR
We implement SCAR (Supernode-Constrained Allocation
for Resource-aware pruning), a one-shot structured pruning
rule that excludes supernodes from the candidate prune set,
ranks all remaining FFN channels by a chosen importance
score, and selects channels under a global sparsity budget
while enforcing per-layer sparsity caps. Halo-aware variants
use redundancy and connectivity only after protecting the
supernode core.
Scoring variants.
SCAR-LP prunes the lowest-LPi non-
supernode channels and therefore tests the value of core
protection alone. SCAR-Prot weights LPi by a redundancy-
based protection score Protecti. SCAR-Conn further incor-
porates connectivity, so that redundant halo channels are
preferentially removed.
The algorithm is detailed in Algorithm 1 (Appendix). Here,
the pruning results serve mainly as evidence about the un-
derlying structure.
6.2. Experimental Setup

6.4. Supernode Ablation: Direct Test of Core Removal
The main comparison suggests that supernode hit-rate is a
key variable. Here we test that more directly by changing
the protected set and by exposing supernodes to pruning
on purpose. We isolate this dependence through three con-
trols: changing the protected set, forcing direct supernode
removal, and comparing against random protection.
Dependence on correct supernode identification.
All
SCAR variants depend on correctly identifying supernodes
via the loss proxy (LP). SCAR-LP scores channels by LP
alone, SCAR-Prot multiplies LP by a redundancy-based
protection term, and SCAR-Conn additionally uses connec-
tivity. At this sparsity, the key benefit of the LP-defined
core is avoiding direct supernode hits; once that core is
protected, fine distinctions among many non-core channels
matter much less.
Direct ablation control.
Appendix Table A5 directly tests
the role of supernodes: removing supernodes first causes
catastrophic failure, while protecting them enables aggres-
sive pruning.
Random supernode control.
As a secondary clarifica-
tion, Appendix Table A5 shows that random protection can
appear competitive at 50% sparsity in some settings because
many LP-supernodes already have scores far above the prun-
ing threshold. This does not eliminate the need to identify
supernodes: when masks are forced to hit the LP-defined
core, perplexity degrades catastrophically. The failure mode
is direct supernode removal.

8. Limitations
Several limitations remain. Supernode identification de-
pends on calibration data, so large distribution shifts may
require re-estimating the scores even if the phenomenon of
extreme concentration still appears. We study FFN channels
because the effect is clearest there; we do not test whether
analogous loss-critical cores exist in attention blocks or
MoE experts. LP is also a Fisher/Gauss–Newton approxi-
mation and may miss nonlinear or non-Gaussian effects.
There are also scope limitations. Although we include tar-
geted 70B validation, the most complete benchmark cover-
age is still at 7–8B scale. The OLMo checkpoint analysis
is observational. It shows that LP concentration is acquired
during pretraining, but it does not identify the training mech-
anism that creates supernodes. Finally, we do not directly
evaluate quantization, fine-tuning, or downstream model-
editing interventions. These are natural applications of the
supernode lens, but they are beyond what the present exper-
iments establish.

9. Conclusion
We identify a small loss-critical core within LLM FFN lay-
ers. Under a Fisher-style activation-gradient proxy, channel-
level sensitivity is highly concentrated, and direct ablations
show that removing this core is far more damaging than
removing matched non-core channels. In one-shot struc-
tured FFN pruning, a major failure mode is direct supernode
removal; protecting these channels explains much of the
robustness gap between SCAR and several channel-pruning
baselines. Halo structure provides a secondary ranking sig-
nal around the protected core, but it is not the main driver of
pruning failure. The same LP-concentration pattern appears
across several model families, remains visible at 70B scale,
and emerges during OLMo-2 pretraining. These results
suggest that LLM FFNs develop a highly skewed channel-
importance geometry, placing activation outliers and super
weights alongside a structured channel-level counterpart that
can be measured, protected, and potentially shaped during
training.
Impact Statement
This paper studies reliability in structured pruning for large
language models. More reliable pruning can reduce memory
use and computational cost, making models cheaper to run
and easier to analyze. These efficiency gains may support
beneficial uses, while also lowering barriers to misuse. Our
contribution is analytical and methodological rather than
application-specific; its broader impact depends on how
improved compression methods are deployed.

Abstract: We study the organization of channel-level im- portance in transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs). Using a Fisher-style loss proxy (LP) based on activation-gradient second moments, we show that loss sensitivity is concentrated in a small set of channels within each layer. In Llama- 3.1-8B, the top 1% of channels per layer accounts for a median of 58.7% of LP mass (range: 33.0– 86.1%). We call these loss-critical channels su- pernodes. Although FFN layers also contain strong activation outliers, LP-defined supernodes overlap only weakly with activation-defined out- liers and are not explained by activation power or weight norms alone. Around this core, we find a weaker but consistent halo structure: some non-supernode channels share the supernodes’ write support and show stronger redundancy with the protected core. We use one-shot structured FFN pruning as a diagnostic test of this organiza- tion. At 50% FFN sparsity, baselines that prune many supernodes degrade sharply, whereas our SCAR variants explicitly protect the supernode core; the strongest variant, SCAR-Prot, reaches perplexity 54.8 compared with 989.2 for Wanda- channel. The LP-concentration pattern appears across Mistral-7B, Llama-2-7B, and Qwen2-7B, remains visible in targeted Llama-3.1-70B exper- iments, and increases during OLMo-2-7B pre- training. These results suggest that LLM FFNs develop a small learned core of loss-critical chan- nels, and that preserving this core is important for reliable structured pruning.
